definition: The way in which a word or language is spoken
etymology: From Latin pronuntiatio, from pronuntiare (to proclaim)
contextSentence: So we're looking at pronunciation.

definition: A speech sound made by partially or fully obstructing airflow, or a letter representing such a sound
etymology: From Latin consonans, from con- (together) + sonare (to sound)
contextSentence: You can connect consonant to consonant.

definition: A speech sound made with an open vocal tract, or a letter representing such a sound (A, E, I, O, U)
etymology: From Old French vouel, from Latin vocalis (vocal)
contextSentence: A vowel is A, E, I, O, U.
contextSentenceKo: 모음은 A, E, I, O, U입니다.

definition: A unit of pronunciation having one vowel sound, forming the whole or part of a word
etymology: From Greek syllabe, from syn- (together) + lambanein (to take)
contextSentence: A syllable is the vowel sounds in a word.
contextSentenceKo: 음절이란 단어 안의 모음 소리를 말합니다.

definition: To pronounce words clearly and distinctly
etymology: From Latin enuntiare, from e- (out) + nuntiare (announce)
contextSentence: We have a word called enunciate.

definition: To give special importance or stress to something
etymology: From Greek emphasis, from en- (in) + phainein (to show)
contextSentence: If you want to emphasize something.

definition: To press firmly together; in this context, to compress words or sounds
etymology: From Old English cwysan (to squeeze, crush)
contextSentence: You're squeezing them together, you're connecting them.

definition: To mix or merge smoothly together
etymology: From Old Norse blanda (to mix)
contextSentence: Say it quickly, blend the letters one into the next.
contextSentenceKo: 빨리 말하면서, 글자들을 하나씩 다음 글자에 섞어보세요.

definition: A person who has spoken a particular language since early childhood
etymology: Native from Latin nativus (born); speaker from Old English sprecan (to speak)
contextSentence: A little bit more like a native speaker, hopefully.

definition: To move smoothly and continuously in one direction
etymology: From Old English flowan (to flow, stream)
contextSentence: So one word flows into the next word.
contextSentenceKo: 그래서 한 단어가 다음 단어로 자연스럽게 이어집니다.

definition: The activity of writing down words that are spoken aloud
etymology: From Latin dictatio, from dictare (to say repeatedly)
contextSentence: What you can do is you can try to do dictation.
contextSentenceKo: 여러분이 할 수 있는 것은 받아쓰기를 해보는 것입니다.

definition: The muscular organ in the mouth used for tasting, speaking, and swallowing
etymology: From Old English tunge (tongue, language)
contextSentence: But according to the tongue and the mouth, they almost sound the same.
contextSentenceKo: 하지만 혀와 입의 움직임에 따르면, 거의 같은 소리가 납니다.

definition: Providing physical ease and relaxation; used here as a key pronunciation example
etymology: From Old French conforter (to comfort) + -able
contextSentence: I've heard many students say comf-or-ta-ble.
contextSentenceKo: 많은 학생들이 comf-or-ta-ble이라고 발음하는 것을 들었습니다.

definition: A word used instead of a noun, such as I, me, my, mine
etymology: From Latin pronomen, from pro- (for) + nomen (name)
contextSentence: It is not a pronoun. A pronoun is I, me, my, mine.
contextSentenceKo: 그것은 대명사가 아닙니다. 대명사는 I, me, my, mine입니다.

definition: Able to accept or tolerate delays or problems without becoming annoyed
etymology: From Latin patiens, from pati (to suffer, endure)
contextSentence: But it takes time, be patient.

definition: To be easy to say; to sound natural and effortless when spoken
etymology: Figurative expression comparing smooth speech to rolling motion
contextSentence: It just rolls off the tongue just like that.

definition: To divide or disconnect into distinct parts
etymology: From Latin separare, from se- (apart) + parare (to prepare)
contextSentence: Separate the syllable before.

definition: In a natural, normal, or relaxed manner
etymology: From Latin naturalis (by birth, according to nature)
contextSentence: That's how a native speaker would say it naturally.

definition: A settled or regular tendency or practice, especially one that is hard to give up
etymology: From Latin habitus (condition, appearance), from habere (to have)
contextSentence: It's more a habit than anything else.

definition: A piece of audio or video that has been captured for playback
etymology: From Latin recordari (to remember, recall)
contextSentence: Somebody on the recording will say, not at all.
contextSentenceKo: 녹음에서 누군가가 'not at all'이라고 말할 겁니다.
